en: Table of Contents for the *Lüyào hòují* (Later Collection of Essential Vinaya Rules), Recited or Original Text (Excerpted from the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Precepts" of the *Dìchí jìpǐn zhōng púsà jìběn jīng*; therefore, it has been abridged here).
Commentary on the *Púsà jiè jīmó wén* (Ritual Text for the Ordination of Bodhisattva Precepts) (Collected in the *Xùzàngjīng*, Set 61).
Revised Method for Bestowing the Bodhisattva Precepts; Method for Studying the Bodhisattva Precepts;
Ritual for Repentance According to the Brahmajāla Sūtra (extracted from the *Jiājīalüyào guǎngjí*, hence abbreviated here);
*Vinaya Hòují*: Questions and Debates.
The Essential Vinaya Collection:
A Revised Method for Bestowing the Bodhisattva Precepts.

(If any bodhisattvas wish to study the three clusters of pure precepts of a bodhisattva—whether they be lay or ordained—they must first resolve upon supreme enlightenment with a great vow, and then seek out one who is fully endowed with merit, wisdom, and power.)
The Bodhisattva Dharma-preacher first prostrates at [the Buddha’s] feet, bared his right shoulder, knelt with both knees touching the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and made this request.
"Venerable sir, please bear this in mind. I, [name], before you, Venerable sir, beg to receive all the pure bodhisattva precepts.
I pray that you will, out of compassion, grant them to me for a moment without declining due to weariness. (Thus, say three times.)"

(Once the teacher has been invited, one proceeds before the image, burns incense, and pays homage. Alternatively, the pure assembly may chant a hymn of praise for the incense. When the hymn is finished, with single-minded reverence, one faces the Triple Gem of the ten directions and performs prostrations with uplifted devotion.)
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to all Buddhas of the past, throughout the entirety of the past.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to all Buddhas of the future, throughout the entirety of the future.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to all Buddhas of the present, throughout the entirety of the present eon.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to all Honored Dharmas of the past, throughout the entirety of the past eon.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to all the Honored Dharmas of the future world, throughout the limits of the future.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to all the Honored Dharmas of the present world, throughout the limits of the present.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to all the worthy ones and sages of the past throughout the entirety of the past.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to all the worthy ones and sages of the future throughout the entirety of the future.
With single-minded devotion, prostrate to all the worthy ones and sages of the present world throughout the entirety of the present eon.
(Having performed one prostration for each, next descend again with reverence; placing the kneecaps upon the ground before the Buddha image, join the palms and request the teacher.)
"I only pray that the Virtuous One will take pity on me and bestow upon me the pure bodhisattva precepts.

(Having made this request, one should focus the mind on a single object, nurture a pure heart, and reflect thus: "Before long, I shall attain the inexhaustible, immeasurable, and unsurpassed treasury of merit. At that time, the Preceptor should ask:
"Listen, son of good family. Are you a bodhisattva? [He answers: "I am. "Have you made the vow for enlightenment?
[He answers: "I have already made it. "Listen, son of good family. You now wish to receive from me all the training precepts of the bodhisattvas."

He receives all the pure precepts of the bodhisattvas—namely, the morality of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*), the morality of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), and the morality of benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla*).

Such points of training and such pure precepts were fully possessed by all bodhisattvas of the past, will be fully possessed by all bodhisattvas of the future, and are now fully possessed by all bodhisattvas currently existing throughout the ten directions. In these points of training...
"Regarding this dwelling in pure precepts: all bodhisattvas of the past have already trained in them; all bodhisattvas of the future shall train in them;
and all bodhisattvas currently existing throughout the ten directions are training in them now. Are you able to accept them? [He] replied, "I am able to accept them."
(After these three rounds of question and answer, one should next say:

"O Son of the Buddha, you should receive the four unbreakable faiths" (from this point downward, the three sections of taking refuge, repentance, and making vows should all be recited by oneself; if one is unable, the teacher should instruct them).
From this moment until the end of the future, throughout all my lives, I take refuge in the Buddha, I take refuge in the Dharma, and I take refuge in the noble Sangha;
I take refuge in the true Dharma and the precepts. (Recite this three times.)
O Son of the Buddha, next you should repent of the transgressions of the three periods of time.
As for the ten non-virtuous transgressions of body, speech, and mind committed in the past, I vow that they shall never arise again throughout the entirety of the future.

As for the ten non-virtuous transgressions of body, speech, and mind committed in the present, I vow that they shall never arise again throughout the entirety of the future. As for [the ten non-virtuous transgressions of body... committed in the future...
"Regarding the ten evils of speech and mind, I vow that they shall never arise again throughout the limits of the future (recite this three times).
O Son of the Buddha, having thus repented, the three karmas are purified; like clear lapis lazuli, they are luminous both within and without."
Next, one should make the Four Great Vows:
Sentient beings are boundless; I vow to deliver them all. Afflictions are inexhaustible; I vow to sever them all.
Dharma gates are immeasurable; I vow to study them all. The Buddha-way is unsurpassed; I vow to perfect it. (Recite this three times.)
"O Son of the Buddha, having now completed the formulation of the great vows, I shall on your behalf address the Triple Gem to serve as witnesses for your reception of the precepts.
You should listen with single-minded attention and contemplate this with careful reflection.

You should know that when the first announcement is finished, the wondrous and virtuous dharma of the precepts throughout the worlds of the ten directions trembles entirely through the power of mental karma. When the second announcement is finished, the ten..."
The wondrous and virtuous precepts of the worlds of the ten directions are like clouds and like canopies, covering the crown of your head.

Having completed the three recitations of the white [announcement], the wondrous and virtuous precepts of the worlds of the ten directions flow from the aperture at the crown of your head into your body and mind, filling your primary retribution.
Until the end of the future, they shall forever serve as the seed of the Buddha. This is the unconditioned (anabhisaṃskāra) precept-essence, an outflow-free (anāsrava) form-dharma.
This has been attained through the influence of your own superior virtuous mind; therefore, you should receive it with utmost sincerity and veneration.

(At that time, the recipient remains kneeling as before. The preceptor rises from his seat and, before the Buddha image, pays respectful offerings to the Triple Gem currently present throughout the ten directions. Prostrating and joining his palms, he makes the following announcement:)
I look up and address the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas throughout the infinite and boundless worlds of the ten directions:
"Now, within this assembly, there is a certain Bodhisattva who, before me, a certain Bodhisattva, has received the Bodhisattva precepts, having recited them as many as three times.
I act as their witness. I pray that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas throughout the infinite and boundless worlds of the ten directions..."
The Tathāgata is the foremost, true, and holy one; in all times and places, whether manifest or unmanifest, he is the one who has attained perfect awakening regarding all sentient beings.
May he likewise bear witness for this [Name], the Bodhisattva receiving the precepts. (Recite thus three times.)
(Next, he should return to his seat and explain the characteristics of the ten grave precepts, exhorting them to uphold them.
"Good sons, listen! A bodhisattva has ten inexhaustible precepts. If one violates them, it is not the conduct of a bodhisattva."
"You shall lose the forty-two dharmas of the noble ones; you should receive this with careful attention.
From this present body until the attainment of the Buddha-body, throughout the interval between them, you must not intentionally take life. Can you maintain this? (He replies, "I can.")
From this present body until the attainment of the Buddha-body, during the interval between them, you must not intentionally commit theft. Can you maintain this? (He answers: "I can.
From this present body until the attainment of the Buddha-body, during the interval between them, you must not intentionally engage in sexual misconduct. Can you maintain this? (He answers: "I can.")
"From this body until the Buddha-body, during the interval between them, you must not intentionally speak false words. Can you maintain this? (He replies, "I can.
"From this body until the Buddha-body, during the interval between them, you must not intentionally sell alcohol. Can you maintain this? (He replies, "I can.")
"From this body until the Buddha-body, during the interval between them, I shall not intentionally speak of the faults of lay or ordained bodhisattvas.
Can you maintain this? [He] replied, "I can."
From this present body until the attainment of the Buddha-body, during the interval between them, you must not intentionally praise yourself or disparage others.
Are you able to maintain this? (He replies: "I am able.")
"From this present body until the attainment of the Buddha-body, during the interval between them, you must not intentionally harbor stinginess. Can you maintain this? (He replies, "I can.
"From this present body until the attainment of the Buddha-body, during the interval between them, you must not intentionally harbor anger. Can you maintain this? (He replies, "I can.")
From this present body until the attainment of the Buddha-body, during the interval between them, you must not intentionally slander the Triple Gem.
Can you maintain this? (He replies: "I can.")
O Son of the Buddha, having received these ten inexhaustible precepts, the recipient transcends the four māras and overcomes the suffering of the three realms.
From birth to birth, they do not lose these precepts; they constantly follow the practitioner until the attainment of Buddhahood.
You should know that such pure precepts received by a bodhisattva are the most excellent and unsurpassed among all other pure precepts ever received.
It is followed by a treasury of immeasurable and boundless great merit; it is initiated by the most supreme and excellent intention of the mind;
and it is universally capable of eliminating every kind of evil conduct of all sentient beings.
All the vows of individual liberation do not equal even one hundredth part of this bodhisattva vow of ethical discipline;
they do not equal one thousandth part, nor a numerical fraction, nor a calculable fraction, nor a fractional part,
nor a metaphorical fraction, nor even a *upaniṣad* fraction thereof, because it encompasses all great merit.
(The Preceptor and the recipient arise together. They prostrate to the Triple Gem of the ten directions. The pure assembly recites in unison:
The supreme practice of the merit of receiving the precepts, And all boundless, victorious blessings, I dedicate them all:
May all sentient beings drowning in the sea of suffering Swiftly proceed to the Buddha-field of Amitābha.
All Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time, and all Honored Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, [I take refuge in] the Mahāprajñāpāramitā.
(Having completed the prostrations to the Triple Gem, the Bodhisattva receiving the precepts should next express gratitude to the Precept Master and the assembly, and then withdraw with reverence.
The Revised Method for Bestowing the Bodhisattva Precepts.
Postscript:
I have observed that regarding the ordination of bhikṣus, the Vinaya possesses established protocols. Although the five schools differ, they are largely the same with only minor variations;

therefore, one should exclusively follow the *Dharmaguptaka* school, eliminating the redundant texts interpolated later. As for the methods for the bodhisattva’s ordination, the sūtras and śāstras each differ.

The *Brahmajāla-sūtra*, the *Yingluo-jing*, the *Dichizhishi-śīla-sūtra*, as well as the *Cittabhūmi-parīkṣā* and others, differ according to their respective capacities; thus, they vary in detail and brevity.
Consequently, the various commentaries on the essential tenets, teachings, and practices each express their own views and establish additional categories and articles.

Although these works are elegant in diction and thorough in meaning, exhausting every nuance, in some instances the meaning remains obscured by the phrasing, such that they are not even as clear as the original sūtras and śāstras.
The directness and immediacy of these [methods] have now been lost in the tradition of the *Brahmajāla-sūtra* initiation rites; only a mere shadow remains.
Only the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* and the *Ratnakaraṇḍa-avadāna* can be relied upon as authentic sources.

Having respectfully consulted these three works, I have synthesized them into a single format, so that the details may be concise yet balanced, ensuring that both the bestower and the recipient find it clear and simple, thereby avoiding confusion and disorder.
It passed by my ears.
Recorded respectfully by Zhi Xu of Guwu in the late autumn of the fourth year of the Chongzhen era, the Xinwei year.
The Method for Studying the Bodhisattva Precepts, Clarified by the Disciple of the Bodhisattva Precepts, Guwu Zhixu.

This account of receiving the precepts through self-vow before the Buddha originates in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* and is detailed in such scriptures as the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* and the *Ratnaketu-śrī-uttarādhyāya-sūtra*. Now...

Incorporating the practices for reciting the various sūtras, ten general points are set forth: first, adorning the ritual site; second, purifying the three karmas; third, delimiting the boundary; fourth, performing offerings;
fifth, praising, prostrating, and taking refuge; sixth, repenting and eliminating evil offenses; seventh, making a formal announcement and requesting witness;
eighth, correctly reciting the precept sūtra; ninth, making vows and prostrating to the Buddha; tenth, generating aspirations and dedicating merit.

First, adorn the site of practice and dwell in a quiet chamber. Set up an image of Vairocana, or an image of Śākyamuni; it is also acceptable to use a painted image, provided that there is indeed a Buddha image.
One must not offer worship to an image of a bodhisattva alone. Hang banners, light lamps, and present incense and flowers.
One should provide food and drink as an offering for one week, two or three weeks, or even for one year or three years, diligently practicing this during the six periods of the day and night.
If one cannot make offerings every day, one must certainly not omit it on the first day.
Alternatively, one may set a duration based on seeing auspicious signs, or simply cultivate a virtuous intention and practice it for the rest of one's life. If...

Recite it three times during the day and night, or twice, or once; provided that the recitation continues without interruption and is strictly protected against intrusion, one will certainly be taken into the care of all the Buddhas.
Second, regarding the purification of the three karmas:
if one is a renunciant, one must first receive the full precepts (*upasampadā*) or the śrāmaṇera precepts, maintaining them with purity and without transgression.
If one is a layperson, one must first fully receive the five precepts without any violation. Next, one should generate the vast bodhicitta.
Focus the mind. Vowing to perpetuate the lineage of the Buddhas and to deliver all sentient beings, one is then fit to receive the Bodhisattva precepts.
One should do so in a quiet place, having rinsed and purified oneself, wearing robes in accordance with the Dharma, and gathering the mind in right mindfulness.
With no idle speech, one should earnestly maintain the visualization of the Triple Gem and seek their compassionate protection.
On the first day of establishing the boundary, before performing prostrations, one should demarcate the boundaries of the practice site according to the Dharma.
Using the supreme divine mantra, the Mahāsitātapatra, one should empower pure water with it and sprinkle it [upon the site].
The boundary is established in the four directions. For those who practice this throughout their lives, there is no fixed altar or site;
it is sufficient simply to circumambulate the image at each session, walking and reciting the mantra once. As the Sūtra says:
"Wherever this mantra exists, an area of twelve yojanas becomes a consecrated boundary. If laypeople are unable to recite the full mantra, they may use the Great Compassion [Mantra].
A divine mantra may also be used.
Fourth, regarding the practice of making offerings:

after the practitioner has established the boundary according to the ritual, they should first spread out their seat before the honored image and stand with palms joined. Then, with a sincere mind, they should direct their attention...

Visualize all the infinite and inexhaustible Triple Gems of the ten directions and the three periods of time, giving rise to profound faith and understanding as if they were present before one’s eyes.
One should then chant:
"All pay homage with reverence."

With single-minded devotion, prostrate to the Three Jewels that eternally abide throughout the ten directions. (Having performed one prostration, kneel with the right knee on the ground, add incense, and hold up flowers, making this proclamation:
"Holding incense and flowers with solemnity, we make offerings according to the Dharma."
May these clouds of incense and flowers pervade the worlds of the ten directions.

In each and every Buddha-field, may they be adorned with immeasurable fragrances, fulfilling the path of the Bodhisattvas and accomplishing the fragrance of the Tathāgata. (Having finished scattering the flowers, next visualize as follows:)
These fragrant flowers of mine pervade the ten directions, forming subtle and wondrous light-pavilions.
With celestial music and divine precious incense, with celestial delicacies and divine precious robes, there are inconceivable wondrous dharma-dusts. From each single dust mote emerge all dust motes;
from each single dust mote emerge all dharmas. They revolve without obstruction, mutually adorning one another, pervading everywhere.
Before the Triple Gem in the ten directions and before the Triple Gem throughout the dharma-realm of the ten directions, my own body performs offerings everywhere;
each and every one pervades the entire dharma-realm, distinct from one another yet without obstruction.

Until the end of the future, they perform the work of Buddhas, universally permeating all sentient beings within the dharma-realm. Through this permeation, all develop the bodhicitta and enter together into [the state of enlightenment].
Realizing the Buddha-wisdom of Non-arising (Having formed this thought, stand up and chant):
Having made offerings, with all reverence (one prostration).
Fivefold Praise, Homage, and Taking Refuge.
Next, kneeling with the right knee on the ground and joining the palms, one should proclaim:
"The Tathāgata’s wondrous form-body is peerless in the world; it is incomparable and inconceivable. Therefore, I now pay homage."
The form of the Tathāgata is inexhaustible, and his wisdom is likewise so; all phenomena are eternally abiding, and for this reason I take refuge.
Having thoroughly subdued the faults of the mind and the four types of bodily [faults], he has reached the inconceivable stage; therefore, I now pay homage to him.
Knowing all phenomena as they truly are, your body of wisdom is unimpeded; you never forget the Dharma—therefore, I now pay homage to you.
I bow to the one who has transcended the immeasurable; I bow my head to the peerless one; I bow my head to the sovereign of the Dharma; I bow my head to the one who has surpassed conceptual thought.
Have compassion and protect me, causing the seeds of the Dharma to grow, so that until my final body, I may always remain before the Tathāgata.
By the power of these roots of goodness from the meritorious deeds I have cultivated in this life and in other births, may the Buddha constantly accept and sustain me.
Having finished the praise, perform one prostration. Then, standing up, chant:
"With a single mind, I pay homage to all Buddhas of the past throughout the entirety of the past."
As you prostrate, recite this thought: "The nature of both the one who bows and the object of worship is empty and quiescent; the mutual resonance of cause and response is inconceivable.

My place of practice is like a jewel of Indra, wherein all Buddhas appear as reflections. My own body and shadow appear before all the Buddhas, seeking the Great Precepts and performing the ritual of prostrating at their feet.
Upon reaching the prostrations to the Worthies and Sages, change the two characters for "Buddha" (諸佛) to [the specific name of] the worthy or sage.
Having written the two characters "Worthy Sage" (賢聖),
one should with single-minded devotion pay homage to all Buddhas of the future throughout the limits of the future;
with single-minded devotion, one should pay homage to all Buddhas of the present throughout the limits of the present.
With single-minded devotion, prostrate to all Buddhas of the past throughout the limits of the past.
Contemplate thus: "The true nature of phenomena is like empty space; the eternally abiding Dharma Jewel is inconceivable. My body and shadow appear before this Dharma Jewel;
with single-minded devotion, I take refuge and pay homage according to the Dharma."
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to all the Honored Dharmas of the future world throughout the limits of the future.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to all the Honored Dharmas of the present world throughout the limits of the present.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to all the worthy and holy ones of the past, throughout the entirety of the past.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to all the worthy and holy ones of the future, throughout the entirety of the future.
With single-minded devotion, prostrate to all the worthy and holy ones of the present age throughout the limits of the present.
Having performed one prostration to each, kneel with the right knee on the ground and declare:
"I, the disciple [Name], from this moment until the end of the future, take refuge in the Buddha; I take refuge in the Dharma; I take refuge in the..."
I take refuge in the Sangha of noble sages; I take refuge in the True Dharma and the Precepts. (Recite this three times. Then, prostrate once.
Sixth, the Repentance for Eliminating Evil Offenses:
One should reflect that since beginningless time, one has been deluded regarding one’s own fundamental mind and has committed every kind of evil. One should feel deep self-reproach.
With shame, one shall sever the continuity [of these transgressions] and reproach oneself with earnest sincerity. One should chant with a devoted heart:
"I, disciple [Name], regarding the ten non-virtuous offenses of body, speech, and mind committed in past lives, I pray they may never arise again for as long as the future endures.
Regarding the ten non-virtuous offenses of body, speech, and mind committed in the present life, I pray they may never arise again for as long as the future endures."
[Recite] until the end of time. If there are future offenses of the ten non-virtues of body, speech, and mind, may they never arise again until the end of the future.
Having recited this three times, prostrate once, and then silently contemplate:
"All the evil karma I have created in the past arises from beginningless greed, hatred, and delusion, produced by my body, speech, and mind; all of these I now confess."
Having thus reflected, he thought to himself that his karmic obstacles had been extinguished and his body and mind were as pure as lapis lazuli.
He then performed seven prostrations to request witness,
remained kneeling as before, and with a sincere heart, spoke these words:
I look up to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the assembly of all Bodhisattvas who have entered the great stages.

Now, in the worlds of the ten directions, before the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, I vow to receive all the bodhisattva training rules and all the bodhisattva pure precepts—namely, the morality of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*), the morality of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), and the morality of benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla*). Thus shall I train.
Regarding these training rules and this pure ethical discipline: all bodhisattvas of the past have already fulfilled them; all bodhisattvas of the future shall fulfill them;
and all bodhisattvas currently existing throughout the ten directions are now fulfilling them. Regarding these training rules and this pure ethical discipline:
all bodhisattvas of the past have already trained in them; all bodhisattvas of the future shall train in them; and throughout the ten directions...
Presently existing, all Bodhisattvas now train [in this]. I pray that all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas— the foremost true sages throughout the boundless and limitless worlds of the ten directions,
who have attained manifest awakening at all times and in all places regarding all sentient beings,
whether visible or invisible— may act as witnesses for this disciple, [named] So-and-so, as he receives the Bodhisattva precepts.
Having recited this three times, one prostrates once. If it is a regular daily practice, it may also be recited once.
One should either recite the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* while kneeling upright before an image, or set up a small seat beside the image, sit upon it, and recite; or else, if one is able—
One may recite this from memory or while walking in meditation; however, one must still offer incense and pay respectful homage.
First, one should join the palms and recite three times:
"Namo to the Buddha Vairocana, the Teacher of the Brahma Net Sūtra."

The unsurpassed, most profound, and subtle Dharma, Difficult to encounter in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas— I have now seen, heard, and received it for upholding; May I understand the Tathāgata’s true meaning.
Next, recite the "Mind-Ground" chapter of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*. One may recite both the upper and lower fascicles in their entirety, or recite only the lower fascicle.
Or, divide the latter fascicle into two, three, or even up to six sessions, reciting according to one's capacity.
While reciting, ensure that the characters and phrases are distinct and free from errors or omissions.
Having completed the ninefold prostration and recitation of the sutra, one must further offer incense in reverence. Kneeling before the image, first recite three times:
"Namo to our Original Teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha. (Then, make the vow:)
Regarding these categories of precepts, I now vow before all the Triple Gem to receive, uphold, and practice them.

Until the end of the future, I shall never again abandon them. Even if, for the sake of upholding these precepts, I must endure suffering and hardship throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas.
I vow that for the sake of avoiding suffering, I shall not retreat from or lose today’s resolve for the Way.

Even if, due to the causes and conditions of breaking the precepts, I were to constantly experience peace and happiness for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, I vow that for the sake of such happiness, I shall not retreat from or lose today’s resolve for the Way.
By the merit of training in these precepts, I pray that all the various sins committed by myself and all sentient beings since beginningless time may be completely extinguished.
If there be any determinate karma among all sentient beings that must be experienced as retribution, I shall receive it all on their behalf.

Throughout lands as numerous as motes of dust, traversing all evil realms for kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, I shall fully endure every kind of suffering, receiving it with joy and patience, never becoming weary or regretful.
May those sentient beings first attain the Way of the Buddha. May my aspiration be true and not false; may the ten directions [bear witness].
The Three Jewels appear before me as witnesses. They stroke my head with their hands, clothe my body with their robes, and anoint me with the nectar of immortality.

Their radiance illuminates my person, causing my resolve for the Way to increase day and night. I enter various samādhis and attain dhāraṇīs. The ocean of Mañjuśrī’s wisdom becomes pure moment by moment;
the ocean of Samantabhadra’s conduct is perfected thought after thought. After the end of this life, may I be reborn in...
Before the Buddha, they realize the inconceivable realm of liberation and are able to sport freely within it;

they enter and emerge from the toils of worldly existence to fully deliver the stream of deluded beings, so that all may ascend together to the shore of enlightenment. Though empty space may come to an end, my vows shall never cease. I take refuge and pay homage with my head bowed to the Triple Gem.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to Vairocana Buddha, the Teacher of the Brahma Net Sutra (three prostrations).
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to our Original Teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to Amitābha Buddha of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the Buddha Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the seven Buddhas of the past and the ten Buddhas of the ten directions.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the thirty-five Buddhas, the fifty-three Buddhas, and the one hundred and seventy Buddhas.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the thousand Buddhas of the Adorned Eon, the thousand Buddhas of the Auspicious Eon, and the thousand Buddhas of the Constellation Eon.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to all Buddhas throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate three times before the subtle and honored Dharma of the "Bodhisattva’s Mind-Ground Chapter" of the Brahma Net Sūtra.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate before the Vinaya Piṭakas of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, as well as all honored Dharmas throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Huantong Huaguangzhu.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Huaguangwang Dazhiming.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva; Vajragarbha Bodhisattva; and Ākāśagarbha Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva; and Samantabhadra Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya, who is in his final birth before Buddhahood.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to all Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Venerable Upāli, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, the Venerable Ānanda,
and the entire assembly of Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, and noble Saṅgha.

The visualization verses should be understood as they were previously explained. If one performs this as a regular practice, and at times such as when walking on a path or suffering from fatigue and illness, one is unable to perform prostrations, then while engaged in any of the four modes of conduct (īryāpatha), one should simply close the eyes, direct the mind, and form the mental conception of performing prostrations.
The merit of this is no different from prostrating with the five limbs touching the ground.
Having completed the tenfold making of vows,
the dedication of merit, and the worship of the Buddha, one must further offer incense with reverence, kneel with the right knee on the ground and palms joined, and recite these Great Vows.
I prostrate to the Honored One whose three bodies are perfected, The ocean of the awakened nature of all suchness,
Equal to the dharma-realm and as vast as space; To the inconceivable ocean of various adornments and great vows,
Where cause and fruit interpenetrate, And to the ocean of all the bodhisattvas' practices.
I also pay homage to the Tathāgata Amitābha, To Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and Kṣitigarbha.
Out of gratitude for the boundless kindness of my compassionate parents, And out of universal compassion for all realms of sentient beings,
I give rise to a genuine and superior resolve And practice the supreme skillful means of Buddha-recollection (*nien-fo*).
With deep faith in the gateway of the Pure Land’s gathering-in, May my vast vows universally encompass all;
With sublime precepts as the boat and wisdom as the rudder, With skillful means as the sail and the Buddha’s power as the wind,
I shall ferry sentient beings across until the end of the future, Never for a single thought-moment forsaking those in the five turbidities.
The ocean of vows of all Buddhas is like a sovereign jewel, encompassing my own vows which manifest in successive layers;
my vows are likewise like a king of mani-gems, encompassing the entire ocean of vows of all Buddhas.
May this wheel of vows extend horizontally throughout the ten directions and vertically through the three periods of time.
The vehicle upon which the wisdom of all-knowledge rides—therefore, with a sincere heart, I diligently cultivate this foremost vow.
I have given rise to this fundamental resolve, desiring to repay the kindness of my compassionate father who gave me birth.

I pray that by the power of the compassion of the Triple Gem, may all the fathers from whom I have passed through births since beginningless time be born together in the Pure Land, and quickly [attain liberation].
I shall realize Bodhi. May those who hear my name likewise be able to repay the kindness of their fathers.
My second vow is this: when I first resolved to attain enlightenment, it was because I desired to repay the compassionate kindness of my mothers who nurtured me.

I pray that through the compassionate power of the Triple Gem, all the compassionate mothers from whom I have been born throughout beginningless lifetimes may be reborn in the Pure Land and swiftly [attain liberation].
I shall realize Bodhi. May those who hear my name also be able to repay the kindness of their mothers.
My third vow is: I pray that after all sentient beings throughout the entire Dharma-realm and the void-realm have been led to complete Buddhahood, I shall then enter Nirvana.
The fourth vow is: May my own sexual impulses be severed in both body and mind, such that even the nature of severance is non-existent;
and may those who hear my name likewise attain the permanent severance of the root of lust.
The fifth vow is: May my karmic habituation to the act of killing be extinguished without remainder, so that all who hear my name may universally give rise to the power of loving-kindness.
The sixth vow is: May my karmic habituation to the darkness of ignorance and the slandering of the Triple Gem be extinguished without remainder, so that all who hear me...
As for the name: it is the correct faith in the Triple Gem.
The seventh vow is: "May all my unwholesome karmas be completely purified, so that those who hear my name may be enabled [to attain liberation]."
I shall dwell securely in the holy life (*brahmacarya*).

My eighth vow is: may I be reborn with certainty in the World of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*), swiftly realize unexcelled bodhi, and manifest emanations throughout lands as numerous as atoms to liberate sentient beings until the end of the future, without ever becoming weary.
The ninth vow: May I, in birth after birth and life after life, never forget my original vow and skillfully transform sentient beings within the world of the five turbidities.
The tenth vow: May I, wherever I may be, propagate and disseminate the True Dharma, free from all demonic obstacles.
The eleventh vow is: May I attain immeasurable wisdom and be well able to penetrate all Buddha-dharmas.
The twelfth vow is: May I attain immeasurable eloquence to guide the deluded masses, subdue those of external paths, and be entirely fearless, like the roar of a lion.

The thirteenth vow is: May I attain immeasurable supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and travel everywhere to the lands of the ten directions to serve all Tathāgatas and spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), as well as all assemblies of the ocean-like multitude, without failing to do so for even a single moment.

The fourteenth vow is: May I be able to produce various subtle and wondrous sounds, extolling the Triple Gem throughout the bounds of the future, so that all sentient beings may know where to take refuge.

The fifteenth vow is: May I be able to produce all manner of subtle and wondrous offerings at will to make offerings to the Triple Gem, thereby acting as a great field of merit for all sentient beings.
The sixteenth vow: I rejoice in all the merits of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions, so that they may achieve unexcelled bodhi.

Regarding the seventeenth vow: When the Tathāgatas of the ten directions attain perfect enlightenment, I shall first entreat them to turn the Great Wheel of Dharma, revealing the unsurpassed path of awakening to all sentient beings.
The eighteenth vow: When the Tathāgatas of the ten directions enter parinirvāṇa, I shall exhort them all not to enter nirvāṇa, but to remain eternally in the world to benefit all sentient beings.
Regarding the nineteenth vow: among the assemblies of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, they shall designate me as a Great Dharma Prince;
and within all the ocean-like assemblies, the Buddhas shall praise my merit, wisdom, compassion, and power of vows as being no different from those of Avalokiteśvara or Kṣitigarbha.

The twentieth vow is: I vow that with the light of great compassion, I shall illumine all the hells; may those who come into contact with my light have their various sufferings transformed into supreme and wondrous bliss at that very moment.
The twenty-first vow: I vow that with the light of great compassion, I shall illumine all hungry ghosts.
May those who come into contact with my light immediately cast off their bodies as hungry ghosts and attain rebirth in the Pure Land.
The twenty-second vow: May I, through the light of great compassion, illumine all animals;
may those who receive my light be freed from all fears, and after they cast off their bodies, attain rebirth in the Pure Land.
The twenty-third vow is: I vow that with the light of great compassion, I shall illumine all ghosts and spirits.
May those who receive my light completely abandon their hearts of anger, awaken to the Buddha-way, cast off all ugliness, and attain pure bodies.
The twenty-fourth vow is: I vow that with the light of great compassion, I shall illumine all sentient beings suffering in affliction.

May those who receive my light have their illnesses eliminated, may their six sense faculties become complete, and may they be liberated from all perils and hardships. May all immeasurable terrors be cast away;
may they be free from disease and enjoy long lives, and may they resolve to attain Bodhicitta. Should they approach the end of their lives, they shall immediately be reborn in the Pure Land.

The twenty-fifth vow is: I vow that with the light of great compassion, all beings—whether with form or without form, with thought or without thought, as well as all demons and outsiders—shall be touched and illumined, causing their bodies and minds to abandon all false views and attain penetration into the Buddha-vehicle.

The twenty-sixth vow is: I vow that by the light of great compassion, I shall illumine and touch humans and devas, causing them not to be deluded by sensual pleasures or the delight in meditative absorption, so that each may diligently seek unsurpassed bodhi.

The twenty-seventh vow is: I vow that by the light of great compassion, I shall illumine all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, causing them to relinquish their realization of the unconditioned and swiftly hasten toward the Buddha Vehicle.

The twenty-eighth vow is: I vow that with a voice of great compassion, I shall reveal and instruct all sentient beings, causing them to attain definitive and clear awakening, so that they no longer cling to the three realms, take no pleasure in other vehicles, and seek only unsurpassed bodhi.

The twenty-ninth vow is: I vow that by the power of my great compassion, I shall accord with the various requests of sentient beings and always cause them to have their wishes fulfilled, so that they may develop deep faith in my Dharma.
Regarding the thirty vows: for the sake of saving and delivering sentient beings, I vow to manifest as a Buddha-body throughout the ten directions.
I shall either manifest pure lands to gather in sentient beings, adorned with such supreme excellence that they surpass even the Land of Ultimate Bliss;
or I shall manifest defiled lands to transform and guide sentient beings, employing immeasurable skillful means to subdue evil associates.
Regarding the thirty-first vow: For the sake of delivering sentient beings, I vow to manifest my body in accordance with their various types.
Within each type, I shall be of noble lineage and preeminent status, possessing sovereign majesty and virtue, so that all who share my kind may revere and love me;
following my instructions, they shall proceed directly to Bodhi.

Regarding the thirty-two vows: in all places where there is no Buddha-dharma, in all places where all dharmas have perished, and in all places where the Buddha-dharma cannot be practiced, I vow to manifest my body therein through the skillful means of great compassion.

By alternating concealment and appearance, I shall perform a great transformation, acting as a lamp for the long night to rescue those submerged in darkness and deliver them from the sea of suffering.
Regarding the thirty-three vows: may I always manifest as food and drink when sentient beings are hungry and thirsty;
as medicinal herbs during epidemics; as clothing in times of cold and frost; as a cooling breeze during times of heat and affliction;
and as ferries and bridges at places of peril and obstruction—indeed, may I provide for all that sentient beings require.

I manifest these forms so that all sentient beings—whether they consume them as medicine or food, or rely upon them by leaning against or treading upon them—may all attain peace and happiness, and give rise to the bodhicitta.
Regarding the thirty-four vows: if there are sentient beings who joyfully seek the Buddha-vehicle and, having heard my name, do not abandon their bodies...
Body. Attaining the Bodhi of a Buddha and realizing the ultimate.

Regarding the thirty-five vows: if there are bodhisattvas who adorn buddha-lands and, upon hearing my name, find their lands to be more sublime and wondrous than Sukhāvatī, yet wish to manifest in impure lands, they shall obtain immeasurable skillful means to effectively transform those who are stubborn and difficult to guide.
To transform sentient beings:
regarding the thirty-six vows, if there are sentient beings who wish to see the pure lands of all Buddhas and hear the sound of their preaching the Dharma,
I vow that they shall all obtain such vision and hearing.

Regarding the thirty-seven vows: if there are sentient beings who wish to travel to countless worlds to make offerings to the Triple Gem, may they be able to reach them all universally within a single moment of thought.

Regarding the thirty-eighth vow: If there are sentient beings who wish to be born in the pure lands of the Buddhas and hear my name, they shall immediately attain rebirth there in accordance with their vows.
The thirty-ninth vow: If there are sentient beings who share my vow, may they swiftly attain immeasurable wisdom, skillful means, and sovereign majestic power.

Regarding the forty vows: If there are sentient beings who delight in seeking the Lesser Vehicle, I vow that they shall swiftly attain the fruits of sainthood and immediately turn their minds toward entering the Bodhisattva Vehicle.
The forty-first vow: I vow that all bodhisattvas practicing throughout the ten directions, upon hearing my name, shall proceed directly to Bodhi without ever encountering demonic obstacles.

Regarding the forty-second vow: I vow that all heterodox spirits and followers of external paths throughout the ten directions, upon hearing my name, shall immediately abandon their false views and together return to true enlightenment.

Regarding the forty-third vow: If there are sentient beings who have committed the five heinous crimes and the ten evil deeds, or the four and eight abandonments, and are destined to fall into the great hells, I vow that by the power of my great compassion, they shall be made to know how to seek pity and repent.

I will manifest a supreme and wondrous form-body before those individuals, touch their heads to comfort them, and cause the roots of their offenses to be forever uprooted, so that they may resolve to attain Bodhi.
Focus the mind.

Regarding the forty-four vows: if there are sentient beings who either slander my Dharma or revile my name, although their karmic obstructions are heavy, I vow that by the power of my impartial great compassion, I shall cause them to extinguish their evils and swiftly hasten toward Bodhi.
Regarding the forty-fifth vow: May my eyes of compassion be supremely pure, universally beholding the entirety of the realm of empty space;
may all beings, even those in places of extreme suffering, be brought to peace and happiness, and may all most wicked sentient beings be made virtuous and good.
The forty-sixth vow is: May my hand-seal be supremely adorned, such that in every thought-moment it produces clouds of all manner of offerings,
clouds of various precious jewels, clouds of various garments, clouds of various utensils, clouds of various food and drink, clouds of various medicines,
clouds of various samādhis, clouds of various dhāraṇīs, clouds of various eloquence, and clouds of various illuminations.
Like clouds, they pervade the realm of empty space, benefiting sentient beings until the end of the future, without interruption.
Regarding the forty-seven vows: may my name be most supreme and far-reaching, pervading the entirety of the ten directions without exception;
even to the places where the Dharma has perished, may my name not cease to exist. May I always cause all sentient beings, whether they hear it or recite it, to [attain... entirely.
Attaining liberation.

Regarding the forty-eight vows: I vow that my physical body shall be supremely subtle and refined, adorned by the marks of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*) as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields; and in each individual mark, there shall be [unspeakably unspeakable...]
He spoke of the secondary marks (anuvyañjana), as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields.
Each mark possesses rays of light as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable Buddha-fields.
Each ray of light manifests colors as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable Buddha-fields, adorning the realms of the world and all proclaiming that which is unspeakable.
They can proclaim sounds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable Buddha-fields, extolling the sublime Dharma;
they all emit fragrances as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable Buddha-fields, universally perfuming all things;

they all produce exquisite food and drink as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable Buddha-fields, making offerings to all; they all rain down [requisites] as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable...
One may speak of garments and all manner of requisites, as numerous as the atoms within an unspeakably unspeakable number of Buddha-fields, universally bestowed upon all beings.

From each of these, there manifest unspeakably unspeakable numbers of transformation Buddhas, as numerous as the atoms within an unspeakably unspeakable number of Buddha-fields, who teach and transform all beings. Each and every transformation Buddha...
Each was accompanied by a retinue of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.
Each and every Bodhisattva possessed a supreme adornment as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields;
each and every such adornment manifested as [unspeakably unspeakable... Buddha-fields.

The vast Buddha-activities, as numerous as the atoms of dust, each and every one of them benefits sentient beings throughout worlds as numerous as the atoms of dust in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields. Any sentient being who beholds even a single Buddha-activity shall behold my subtle and wondrous form-body;
and those who behold my body shall be able to attain equality with me and quickly realize [enlightenment].
May I attain Buddhahood.
When I am on the verge of death, may all obstacles be completely eliminated;
may I behold that Buddha Amitābha face-to-face and immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
Once I have been reborn in that land, may these great vows be manifested and accomplished before me, all perfectly fulfilled without exception;
may the realms of all sentient beings be benefited and brought joy, and may the assemblies of that Buddha be entirely pure; at that time, may I be born from a supreme lotus flower.
I beheld the Tathāgata of Immeasurable Light, who bestowed upon me the prophecy of enlightenment in his very presence.
Having received that prophecy from the Tathāgata, I manifested hundreds of billions of transformation bodies;
with vast power and wisdom pervading the ten directions, I universally benefit the realms of all sentient beings.
Until the empty space of worlds is exhausted, And until sentient beings, karma, and afflictions are exhausted—
As long as all such things remain inexhaustible, May my vows remain ultimately and eternally inexhaustible.
This vast and sublime vow of mine, I dedicate entirely toward boundless, supreme merit.
May all sentient beings drowning in the sea of suffering Swiftly proceed to the Buddha-field of Amitābha.
All Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time, And all Honored Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
Mahāprajñāpāramitā. (Then rise and recite the Three Refuges.)
Taking refuge in the Buddha, may all beings realize the Great Way and give rise to the unsurpassed mind.
Taking refuge in the Dharma, may all beings enter deeply into the treasury of the scriptures, their wisdom as vast as the ocean.
Taking refuge in the Sangha, may all beings lead the great assembly with total unimpededness.
The method for bowing to the noble assembly and making vows is as follows: each may act according to their preference.

Whether one wishes to study the forty-eight vows of Amitābha Buddha, the twelve great vows of Bhaisajyaguru Tathāgata, or the ten kings of vows of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, one may do so according to one's inclination.
When employing them, it is not necessarily required that one rely exclusively on these specific vows.

Furthermore, if one wishes to make various other aspirations according to one's own inclinations—whether extensive or concise—it is likewise permissible, provided they are consistent with the Four Great Vows.
There is no fault in this; let those who study well choose for themselves.
These rules for training in the precepts were definitively engraved into the *Vinaya Hòují* (Supplementary Collection on the Vinaya) during the summer of the Wùchén year.
Now, in the summer of the Guīwèi year, I have revised one or two points once again and appended them here following the *Fǎnwǎng Hézhù* (Combined Commentary on the Brahmajāla Sūtra).
Hereafter, these shall be taken as the standard. Written with reverence by Ouyi Zhixu.
From the *Posterior Collection of Questions and Debates on the Bodhisattva Śīla-dharma-vinaya*: Question.
The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states: "If one preaches the precepts taught by the Seven Buddhas before a person who has not yet received the precepts, one commits a minor offense."

It is a transgression. If you claim that this prohibition applies only to the time of recitation and not to the time of exposition, consider this: at the time of recitation one merely proclaims the words and phrases, whereas at the time of exposition one fully explains the principles and meanings.
To value the fishing trap while slighting the fish—what intent could there be in such a view?

Answer: Regarding the monastic precepts (bhikṣu-śīla), because they pertain to the Saṃgha’s wheel and are intended to prevent those who "dwell like thieves" from joining, all such matters are prohibited.

Regarding the Bodhisattva precepts, which universally encompass beings of the five destinies, the understanding of their meaning and the arousal of the bodhicitta are not forbidden. However, when reciting the precepts, there may be instances requiring disclosure and repentance;
since it is improper to allow those who have not yet received the precepts to know of these matters, it is said that one must not speak of them.

Question: The *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* (Bodhisattva-jie ben) lists only four grave offenses (*catvāraḥ pārājikāḥ*), whereas the *Brahmajāla-sūtra* extensively explains ten grave offenses. Thus, there is a difference between the detailed and the concise.
Furthermore, according to the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*, one who commits one of the ten grave offenses must necessarily see auspicious signs (*lakṣaṇa*) before being permitted to receive the precepts again.

The *Śīla-sūtra*, however, simply states that if one loses the bodhisattva precepts, they should be received again. There is thus a distinction between the lenient and the strict. Of these two scriptures, which is the original?
The Master and Upādhyāya proclaim this; it is the personal instruction of the Precept-Conferring Ācārya. These should not contradict one another.
How, ultimately, are they to be reconciled? Answer:

The *Śīla-sūtra* (Prātimokṣa) is derived from the *Bodhisattva-bhūmi*. In the *Bodhisattva-bhūmi*, killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying are collectively termed the "Eight Grave Offenses" (*aṣṭau gurukāpatti*) of the renunciant.

In the *Sūtra on the Questions of Sujāta*, killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, selling intoxicants, and slandering are enumerated as the six grave precepts (*ṣaḍ-guruka-śīla*) for an upāsaka.
The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* encompasses the meaning of both these sūtras and establishes them collectively as ten grave precepts; the *Ratnaketu-dhāraṇī-sūtra* (Yíngluò) is likewise.

This difference between the detailed and the concise arises because the capacities of those to whom they are addressed are not equal. Now, the *Prātimokṣa* lists only four matters, which further possesses three meanings.
First, regarding those living at home who wish to receive these precepts, they must have already previously received the five precepts.

Regarding those who have left the home life and wish to receive these precepts, they must have already previously received the ten precepts and the full set of precepts (*śīla*). Since killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying are fundamental and grave offenses, they need not be listed again;
therefore, only this superior code of discipline (*adhiśīla*) is enumerated here. Second, as for the Bodhisattva precepts, whether in the case of transgression or compliance...
For the sake of sentient beings, it may be permissible to manifest minor forms of natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).

However, regarding these four precepts, there is no logical basis for granting such exemptions; therefore, they are listed separately. Third are the four root offenses (*mūlāpatti*); once committed, one falls into ruin forever.

This principle was already clarified when receiving the five precepts, the ten precepts, and the full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*). Although the Mahāyāna teachings generally permit repentance, it must necessarily involve the manifestation of signs (*nimitta*).

Regarding these four dharmas: although one who commits them loses the precepts, they are still capable of receiving them again. Fearing that this might be confused with the previous four [grave offenses], they are listed separately.

If the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states that one who has committed a grave offense must see auspicious signs [to be reinstated], this is precisely because Śākyamuni was the Preceptor (*upādhyāya*) for the Great Precepts;

as he established the rules, they could not help but be strictly formulated. However, since Maitreya acts as the Preceptor for the conferral of the precepts (*karmācārya*), [the requirements] are lighter.
Regarding the re-opening of prohibitions and permissions, the principle must be examined in detail. Now, one should clarify this by synthesizing the various sūtras and śāstras.

It should be understood that if any one of the four [offenses]—killing, stealing, and so forth—is committed, all the precepts are forfeited; however, upon seeing an auspicious sign, they may be solemnly received again.

Yet, within the dharma of a bhikṣu, one still lacks the capacity for monastic functions. As for the six [offenses] beginning with selling alcohol, if any one is committed, the bodhisattva precepts are lost.
For those with the full precepts and below, this is not termed a "loss"; therefore, they are permitted to repent with earnestness and receive the precepts again.
This is why these two sūtras supplement one another by implication; they are not contradictory.
Question: Within the Dharma of the bhikṣus, prohibitions (pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya) may be waived when there are difficult circumstances.

Now, regarding the Mahāsattva’s discipline, for the sake of benefiting others, there are waivers for natural offenses (prakṛti-sāvadya), yet there is no textual authority for waiving prohibited offenses. What is the meaning of this? Furthermore, regarding the two modes of practice—contrary and conformable—if one has attained the stage of an Ārya, then both self and others can be benefited.
However, if one is an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) at the beginning of their training, the power of body and mind is weak; even for oneself, [one is still unable...]
If there is deficiency, how can one benefit others? Or if one calls oneself a Bodhisattva, using compassion as a pretext to act according to one's own desires—is this not a transgression?

Answer: Prohibitive offenses (*pratikṣepa-śikṣāpada*) are for the sake of protecting sentient beings; all Mahāsattvas should study them together. However, those who abide in little benefit, little activity, and little practice...

Regarding the skillful means (*upāya*): these are not shared with those in training (*śaikṣa*). If they are permitted due to difficult circumstances, since one has already been training equally with the *śrāvakas*, why would it be necessary to permit them further?

It is only for this category of natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), which are exclusively prohibited, that permission is required. Within the context of such permitted exceptions, there is no distinction made between ordinary beings and sages;

provided that the result is the emergence of compassion, the vow to take upon oneself the suffering of others, and the deep arising of shame and remorse, performed without regarding it as a personal achievement, [the act is permissible].

Thus, the aggregate of precepts remains intact. If, however, you make excuses under the guise of travel and act according to your own whims and passions, you will merely deceive yourself and inevitably impair the essence of the precepts.
Do not covet the hollow reputation of a Great Being at the cost of inviting the bitter retribution of the long night.

Question: In the *karmavācanā* text for receiving the precepts, it is stated that if there is no preceptor, one may receive them before an image of the Buddha; this is the "self-vow" method of receiving the precepts according to the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*.
It further specifies that one must necessarily perceive a "good sign" (*lakṣaṇa*), and if such a sign is not perceived, it is not called "attaining the precepts.
How, then, can this be reconciled?
Answer: Regarding the single matter of receiving the precepts, one must discuss both the causes and conditions. The cause consists of the earnestness of the inner mind;

the condition consists of the clarity of the transmission from teacher to recipient. From the perspective of cultivation and realization (*bhāvanā-sākṣātkriyā*), the depth of the cause is valued; from the perspective of the path of teaching (*śāsana-mārga*), the completeness of the conditions is required.
Therefore, the *Bhikṣu-vinaya-piṭaka* strictly maintains the essence of the Sangha Jewel by emphasizing the collective conditions, while the *Bodhisattva-bhūmi-alaṃkāra* opens the way toward Bodhi.

To lead them along this path, one should simply observe the original ground. In the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, when the precepts were first established, it was necessary that two methods support one another;

therefore, although self-administration of the precepts is permitted, it must necessarily be contingent upon the presence of a witness. Furthermore, one should know that as explained in the *Awakening of Faith*:
There may be sentient beings who, out of great compassion, are able to spontaneously generate the resolve [for awakening].

Or, because the True Dharma is about to perish, they are able to spontaneously generate the resolve through the causal conditions of protecting the Dharma. Furthermore, there are those who generate that resolve upon seeing the physical marks of a Buddha.
Now, the Brahmajāla Sūtra prescribes seeking to see auspicious signs (*lakṣaṇa*), thereby causing them to aspire toward Bodhi. The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* permits this through images.

Regarding "receiving [the precepts] previously," this refers exclusively to those who have already generated the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*). Thus, the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* strictly regulates the establishment of the dharma, while the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* strictly regulates the selection of the person;
these two also serve as a mutual complement. Furthermore, the *Ratnakaranda-śrāvakācāra Sūtra* states:

"Receiving [the precepts] in the presence of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is called the superior grade of precept (*uttama-śīla*); receiving them from a Dharma Master is called the middle grade of precept (*madhyama-śīla*); [if there is no such teacher] within a thousand *li*..."

The Master [instructs that] one receives it oneself before the image; this is termed the "inferior grade" (adhamā) of precepts. Furthermore, there is no mention of seeking to see auspicious signs (*lakṣaṇa*).

Nevertheless, this has been a general classification based on external conditions. Moreover, another treatise states: "By generating the superior mind (*adhimukti-citta*), one attains the superior precepts.
It further says: "Because the mind is inexhaustible, the precepts are also inexhaustible. Thus, these may also be classified as superior, middling, or inferior based on internal causes.
Furthermore, those who seek the precepts today must examine themselves with great care.

If one can truly ensure that every thought corresponds with compassion and wisdom, bearing the True Dharma upon oneself and taking pity on all living beings below, then one may directly follow the *Yingluo* and *Dichizhi* [Vinaya] systems;

even if one does not encounter a teacher, one may receive them by self-ordination. However, if one merely aspires to the Buddha-way while compassion and wisdom are not yet profound, then one must uphold the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* (Fanwang) method.
If there is no teacher for a thousand *li*, one must seek out those with auspicious marks.

Furthermore, if a clear and enlightened teacher is currently present, yet one harbors arrogance in the heart and refuses to seek instruction from them, instead seeking it from an image—this is something both scriptures strictly forbid; the five repentances will ultimately fail to achieve success.
Since one desires to hasten toward the ultimate fruit, how can one allow the causal ground to be untrue? It is most inappropriate for a man of talent and resolve to deceive or delude himself.
Question: The Mahāyāna places primary emphasis on internal causes. How can we know that when contemporary Vinaya masters bestow the Bodhisattva precepts upon others?
Regarding the internal cause, whether it is true or not: if it is not true, can it be called "attaining the precepts"?
If one does not attain the precepts, then even if one commits the ten grave offenses, would one still be judged for those ten grave offenses?
Answer: Within the ritual text (*karmavācanā*) for the Bodhisattva precepts, there are fully detailed methods for observing whether a candidate is a suitable vessel.

If one fails to discern these internal causes and transmits the precepts based on superficial appearances, one cannot avoid the fault of acting as a teacher without understanding. As for that recipient of the precepts:

Although one does not generate the precepts within an unwholesome or neutral state of mind, since one has already improperly assumed the name of a bodhisattva, one must naturally judge one's transgressions according to the Dharma;
this is not like the case of the bhikṣu precepts, where one is ultimately treated as a "sneak" (cora-vāsin).
Question: In the *karmavācanā* for repenting transgressions, it is permitted to confess one's faults before those of the Hīnayāna.

However, in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, it is stated that one must not proclaim these Great Precepts of the Thousand Buddhas before someone who has not received the Bodhisattva precepts; indeed, one should not even speak of them to such a person, let alone confess one's faults before them.
How can these two positions be reconciled?
Answer: Although those of the Hīnayāna have not yet received the Bodhisattva precepts, they are members of the Saṃgha who maintain the Dharma and are capable of receiving repentance.
Furthermore, although a Śrāvaka may not yet recognize that the elder is his father, he is in truth the true son of the elder;

he cannot be compared to any other person who has not received the precepts. As for the fortnightly recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), sending such a person away so that he must leave is the *pravāraṇā* (dismissal).
This is the constant rule of the Bodhisattvas; it is also the subtle purport of refuting [wrong views]. One must not cling to this [text] to challenge that [teaching]. Question:
In the first minor precept (*āpatti*) of the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*, it says that upon seeing one’s elders, preceptors (*upādhyāya*), or ācāryas, one should provide offerings according to the Dharma.
Within the forty-one precepts, it teaches that the instructing teacher (*śikṣācārya*) should instruct one to request two teachers. Furthermore, regarding the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*)...
"By slaying two masters, one becomes seven. Now that you receive the Bodhisattva precepts, why do you have only one master?
Once the precepts have been obtained, whom do you designate as your *upādhyāya*?"
Answer: If one follows the wording of the sūtra, it appears that two preceptors are required; however, both the *Ratnakūṭa* (Yingluo) and the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* (Dichi) specify only one.

Furthermore, the method for receiving the vows according to the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, which was transmitted from Master Kumārajīva and recorded in his commentary (*Yishu*), also specifies only one preceptor.

As for the mention of requesting two preceptors, it likely refers to requesting the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Regarding the statement that one "should provide offerings to the two preceptors according to the Dharma," and [the mention of] killing...
If the two masters constitute the offense of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*), then by extension, this could also apply to the two masters for the *bhikṣu* precepts and so forth.

Question: In the ritual for receiving the precepts as reaffirmed here, since the vow for Bodhicitta has already been made during the initial questioning and answering, why is one required to again give rise to the Four Great Vows after the repentance of transgressions? Would this not incur the fault of excessive redundancy?
Answer: The bodhicitta is not to be generated only once; rather, it should be generated repeatedly so that the continuity of the bodhicitta remains uninterrupted.

Moreover, the former [generation] was the causal stage of careful consideration, while the present is the formal ritual. The former was the generation of the mind directed toward the Path, while the present is the armor-like adornment of the vow.
How could this be called redundant? It is just as when one has already requested a teacher previously, yet requests them again before the image; or as when the *śrāmaṇera* vows are conferred...
Regarding the Buddha’s precepts: when questioning about obstacles and difficulties in private, one asks again within the *saṃgha*. Might this also be called "redundant and prolix"?

Question: Since it is said that spiritual capacities and responses differ and the transmission of the Dharma is not uniform, then whether [the procedure] is concise or prolix, neither constitutes a discrepancy.
Furthermore, since it is said that the addition of articles and regulations causes the meaning to be obscured by the text, then returning directly to a single path would be even more painful.
"Excellent! Why need one wait for three schools to form a single system before it can be said to accord with principle and adapt to the occasion?
Answer: "Principle has no manifold causes; the occasion prizes what is appropriate to the circumstances. To follow directly a single path—this explanation is most correct.
However, as capacities differ and habitual tendencies vary, I initially followed the *Karmavācanā* of Maitreya alone, yet often encountered those who resented it as being too..."
Regarding this "abridgment": since the Dharma can be harmonized and integrated, what prevents us from consulting various sources and venturing to reach a compromise?

I have unified the three into one, employing only the established words of the sūtras and śāstras without adding any further literary embellishment. Since the three scriptures are currently all in circulation, I suspect there must be a specific pedagogical necessity at work;
thus, I have merely conformed to the needs of the present moment, not daring to insist that the modern is right and the ancient is wrong. Whether it may be used or not—this is the first point.
Entrusted to future worthies.
*The Later Collection of Questions and Debates on the Essentials of the Vinaya* (End).
